beats.beat: The company operates in two segments: creating infrastructure — railways, bridges, roads — and operating a ready-mix concrete (RMC) plant at Kashimira in Thane district, Maharashtra.

The product list is specific: designing and constructing railway platforms and station buildings, gauge conversion, laying railway tracks, building beam/cantilever/arch/suspension/cable-stayed/truss bridges, and constructing bituminous and concrete roads.

Revenue is won through a tender process: the client floats a tender, the contractor bids, the lowest quote normally wins a Letter of Acceptance, and the contractor deposits a performance guarantee before site handover.
This is a bid-driven, cost-competitive business — what the company sells is not a proprietary product but the ability to price low, deliver on time and execute technically.

The client list is dominated by public bodies: Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai, Western Railway, Central Railway, Mumbai Railway Vikas Corporation Ltd, Mumbai Metropolitan Region Development Authority and Dedicated Freight Corridor Corporation of India Ltd, plus private names like Sky Way Infrastructure, Dev Engineers, GCC Hotel and Krypton Corp.
The concentration is stark: Western Railway alone made up 52% of orders on hand, and the top customers contributed 57% of total revenue in FY2018.

The company describes itself as a major player in Mumbai infrastructure, slowly consolidating in Maharashtra, with a strong order book and long relationships — Western Railway has been a client since 2006.

business.heading: What the company does
business.purpose: Explain the business in plain words: what it sells, to whom, how contracts are won, where it operates, and where the money actually comes from.

beats.beat: Revenue from operations has fallen in each of the five reported years: ₹86.61 crore (FY2014), ₹90.21 crore (FY2015), ₹74.53 crore (FY2016), ₹73.44 crore (FY2017) and ₹60.53 crore (FY2018).
Net profit after adjustments is wildly uneven: ₹0.96 crore (FY2014), ₹0.78 crore (FY2015), ₹0.33 crore (FY2016), ₹0.16 crore (FY2017) — then a jump to ₹3.15 crore in FY2018.

Profit before interest, depreciation and tax — the closest figure the filing gives to EBITDA — moved from ₹7.84 crore (FY2014) to ₹9.46 crore (FY2015), ₹7.83 crore (FY2016), ₹6.76 crore (FY2017) and ₹9.29 crore (FY2018).

The balance sheet is loaded towards short-term debt: short-term borrowings rose from ₹30.82 crore (FY2014) to ₹35.37 crore (FY2018), while long-term borrowings fell from ₹5.87 crore to ₹1.33 crore over the same period.
Total assets grew from ₹70.62 crore (FY2014) to ₹82.32 crore (FY2018), a rise driven mostly by working capital rather than fixed assets — consistent with a contracting business.

The filing itself warns that the company had negative cash flow in recent financial years and that sustained negative cash flow could hurt the business; the actual cash-flow statement figures are not in the supplied excerpts.
A five-year table of revenue, EBITDA, PAT and borrowings is the cleanest way to show this trajectory.

beats.beat: Amit Bholanath Mishra is the sole promoter and Managing Director; he holds 74,95,476 equity shares, or 90.949% of the pre-issue paid-up capital.

The three other whole-time directors — Bharat Kumar Parmar, Shree Prakash Singh and Mukesh Pandey — each hold only 300 shares; the CFO, Anchal Pachori, is a 28-year-old chartered accountant, and the company secretary, Mohit Soni, is 26.
A key managerial person, Hatim Sakerwala, holds 9% of the equity shares as of the date of the draft prospectus.
The DRHP states that no director or promoter is on the RBI list of willful defaulters and that no criminal cases have been filed against any director.

Related-party transactions are disclosed — ₹68.4 lakh of loans taken from KMP/board members in FY2018, ₹57.7 lakh of director remuneration, and ₹324.3 lakh of outstanding payables to related parties as of 31 March 2018 — and the filing concedes such transactions may continue.

Other flags the company itself lists: two companies promoted by the promoter — Al-Noor Chickens Private Limited and A B Magma Automobiles Private Limited — were struck off by the Registrar of Companies in March 2016 for non-operation, and equity shares were issued in the last 12 months at a price that may be lower than the issue price.

beats.beat: The DRHP calls construction a highly fragmented and working-capital-intensive market that contributes around 8% of India's GDP at constant prices.

Demand drivers cited include the 100 Smart Cities Mission, AMRUT, Make in India, Power for All, eased FDI norms in 15 sectors including real estate and construction, rising urbanisation, higher disposable incomes and population growth.

The filing quotes a large infrastructure investment requirement — ₹50 trillion (US$777.73 billion) by 2022 — and says the logistics sector is expected to grow at a 10.5% CAGR from US$160 billion in 2017 to US$215 billion by 2020.

The macro backdrop in the filing is positive: India's GDP growth estimated above 7% in 2017, a working-age population expected to reach 64% by 2021, and India projected to be the world's third-largest middle-class consumer market by 2020.

Against that, the company's own SWOT section lists the industry headwinds it fears: slow pace of government projects, working-capital crunch affecting profitability, and changes in government policies.
Competition is split between organised and unorganised players, which keeps margins and pricing power weak in a tender-driven market.

beats.beat: A B Infrabuild is a Mumbai-based construction contractor that builds railway platforms, station buildings, bridges and roads, and runs a ready-mix concrete plant near Thane.

Its customers are overwhelmingly government bodies — Western Railway, Central Railway, the Municipal Corporation of Greater Mumbai, MMRDA and MRVCL — and it wins work by winning tenders, usually as the lowest bidder.
The company is proposing a public issue of 44,28,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at a price still to be fixed, and says the money will go mainly into working capital.

The rest of the filing is the counterweight to that pitch: one promoter holds 90.949% of the pre-issue company, revenue has fallen in each of the last four years, and the top customer is tied to a single railway zone.

beats.beat: The issue consists of 44,28,000 equity shares of face value ₹10 each; the issue price is not disclosed in the extracted page and is shown as ₹[●].
The lead manager is Mark Corporate Advisors Private Limited and the registrar is Bigshare Services Private Limited.

The stated object of the issue is to meet working capital requirements of ₹1,130 lakh (₹11.3 crore) plus general corporate purposes; the general corporate purposes amount is not disclosed in the excerpts.

The extracted pages do not explicitly show an offer-for-sale component or name a selling shareholder; every clue points to a fresh issue for the company's own balance sheet, but the fresh-versus-OFS split is not spelled out in the provided facts.

The DRHP acknowledges it has not appointed any independent agency to appraise the project, and says there is no monitoring agency for the proceeds — deployment is at the discretion of management and the board, monitored by the audit committee.

offer.heading: What the company is selling and why
offer.purpose: What is being raised, who is selling, how the money will be used, and which intermediaries are running the issue.

beats.beat: Customer concentration: Indian Railways is the largest customer, contributing 57% of FY2018 revenue, and Western Railway alone is 52% of orders on hand; losing that business would cause a significant dip in revenue.

Tender dependence: revenue depends on government and PSU clients accepting the company's bids; if bids are not awarded or are negotiated lower, financial condition suffers — and the company's own SWOT lists the slow pace of government projects as a weakness.
Negative cash flow and receivables: the company had negative cash flow in recent financial years, and failure to recover trade receivables on time could hurt its financial condition.

Working-capital strain: as of 31 March 2018 the company had ₹405.02 lakh of unsecured loans repayable on demand, and the business is inherently working-capital intensive — a crunch could directly hit profitability.

Governance and regulatory exposure: litigation involving the company, promoter and directors is pending at various stages; two promoter companies were struck off by the ROC; and no independent agency has appraised the project or been appointed to monitor the use of proceeds.

beats.beat: The basis-for-issue-price section discloses earnings per share of ₹1.31 (FY2016), ₹0.63 (FY2017) and ₹12.59 (FY2018).
Return on net worth for the same three years is disclosed as 4.14%, 1.97% and 28.14%.
The face value is ₹10 per share, and the DRHP notes the issue price will be a multiple of this face value, with the multiple itself redacted as [●].

A comparison-of-ratios page (page 55) shows two figures that appear to belong to a peer-comparison table — 12.39 and 44.71 — as well as the company's own 28.14 (likely FY2018 return on net worth), but the extract does not name the peer or label the columns.

No named peer list with their P/E, EPS, NAV or RoNW is available in the provided digest, and the issue price is not fixed; an implied price range therefore cannot be honestly computed from these excerpts.
